characters: Okaikoi: a curious nine-year-old Ghanaian boy with short neat hair, wearing a yellow collared school shirt and brown shorts.
Nafisa: his nine-year-old Ghanaian classmate wearing a soft cream headscarf and matching yellow-and-brown school uniform.
Their teacher: a kind Ghanaian woman wearing a cobalt-blue patterned dress.
Okaikoi’s little brother: a five-year-old Ghanaian boy in a red T-shirt and blue shorts.

narrationPlan.voice: A curious boy’s voice for Okaikoi; a clear girl’s voice for Nafisa; a firm, kind teacher voice
narrationPlan.pace: Curious, with a firm tone on the safety page (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A bright, rising tune with a soft electric hum (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on the sources of electrical energy (B3.4.2.1) and electrical safety (B2.4.2.1). The Akosombo Dam on the Volta River makes electricity from flowing water. It is one of the main sources of electricity in Ghana. Teachers should use accurate local facts.
Solar lamps are used in many homes without a grid connection.
Safety is the heart of the story: do not touch bare or fallen wires, do not put things into sockets, and do not touch switches with wet hands.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the safety rules with the electricity company or the school safety adviser.
Check the description of the Akosombo Dam (Volta River, flowing water makes electricity) with a reliable source before release.

teacherGuide.overview: The sun, flowing water and wind are sources of electrical energy, and electricity must be handled safely. Based on NaCCA Science standards on sources of electricity and electrical safety.
beforeReading: Ask: what at home uses electricity? Where does it come from?
whileReading: Pause on page 5 and ask children to say each safety rule.
afterReading: Sort pictures into “sources of electricity” and “things that use electricity”.
discussion: Which sources will not run out?
reflection: Which safety rule will you tell your family?

support: Use pictures and match each rule to a danger sign.
stretch: Research how your community gets its electricity.
Find out why the sun, water and wind are called renewable sources: they can be used again and again and will not run out.

culturalNotes: The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on the sources of electrical energy (B3.4.2.1) and electrical safety (B2.4.2.1). The Akosombo Dam on the Volta River makes electricity from flowing water. It is one of the main sources of electricity in Ghana. Teachers should use accurate local facts.
Solar lamps are used in many homes without a grid connection.
Safety is the heart of the story: do not touch bare or fallen wires, do not put things into sockets, and do not touch switches with wet hands.
localiseThis: Use the real sources of electricity in your community.
Teach children never to experiment with sockets or wires; use only diagrams and low-voltage battery kits with an adult.
